newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan rebels say take key town, thrust north.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels say take key town, thrust north.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic militia said on Wednesday its forces had captured the strategic government-held town of Sarobi east of the capital Kabul and were thrusting north towards a key government airbase.
Taleban forces seized Sarobi, 70 km (44 miles) from Kabul, at about midnight (1900 GMT Tuesday) in a two-pronged assault after resistance died away, Taleban sources in Pakistan said.
There was no immediate independent confirmation that Sarobi had fallen in what would be the latest in a series of spectacular Taleban gains in eastern Afghanistan this month.
It would be a major setback to the Kabul government led by President Burhanuddin Rabbani and to Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, whose Hezb-i-Islami faction had held Sarobi.
Taleban sources said the Islamic rebels were now advancing northwards up the Tagab Valley that leads to the main government airbase at Bagram, 50 km (31 miles) north of Kabul.
"Sarobi has been taken over completely," a Taleban source in the northwestern Pakistani town of Peshawar said. "Now, inshallah (God willing), we will reach Kabul."
Retreating government forces left behind many dead fighters and large quantities of weapons, the source said.
A Pakistan-based Afghan news service, Afghan Islamic Press, said about 50 government fighters were killed. There was no word on Taleban casualties.
Taleban sources said their forces had advanced on Sarobi northwards from Hisarak district in the adjoining Nangarhar province, and westwards along the main Jalalabad-Kabul highway.
Resistance had subsided by sunset on Tuesday while mopping up operations were completed by midnight, Taleban sources said.
On Tuesday, official Kabul Radio said rockets fired by the Taleban killed three civilians and wounded nine in the capital.
The radio, monitored in Islamabad, said the rockets had hit residential areas near Kabul university.
Taleban sources in the eastern city of Jalalabad said a government jet had dropped cluster bombs near the city's airport, but had caused no damage or casualties.
The Islamic rebel force has tightened its grip on eastern provinces this month as part of a drive to seize Kabul, oust Rabbani and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
Kabul radio said government forces had killed 100 rebels and destroyed many military vehicles in Tuesday's battle for Sarobi.
A Taleban transport plane landed at Bagram on Tuesday, but there were conflicting accounts of the incident.

Kabul radio said the Russian-made Antonov-32 plane carrying 33 Taleban and seven Pakistani military men had been hijacked by a "brave mujahid (struggler)" on a flight between the Taleban-held cities of Herat and Kandahar.
Taleban sources confirmed that the plane had landed in Bagram, but said the pilot had defected. They denied any Pakistanis had been on board the aircraft.
Pakistan also denied the report. "This is absolutely untrue. There are no Pakistani military personnel engaged in fighting anywhere in Afghanistan," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
The Afghan government has often accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban. Islamabad denies the charge.
